newsitem.title: TANZANIA: African leaders give Burundi talks ultimatum.
newsitem.headline: African leaders give Burundi talks ultimatum.

text.p: African leaders on Saturday threatened further sanctions if Burundi's military ruler Pierre Buyoya did not open unconditional talks with Hutu rebels within one month.
Defying a U.S. suggestion to ease the embargo, now more than two months old, the regional leaders said they would send a team to Burundi to check on Buyoya's professed commitment to peace talks.

"The summit reiterated that the objective of the sanctions is to serve as an effective means of securing a negotiated settlement between all parties to the conflict," they said in a statement after a nearly six-hour meeting in Arusha.

Ethnic war between Burundi's Tutsi-dominated army and Hutu rebels is killing up to 1,000 people monthly and regional leaders fear the country could go down the same path as Rwanda where up to a million people were killed in genocide in 1994.

Refusing to accept U.S. arguments that steps by Buyoya showed progress that should be rewarded, the regional leaders stressed their main demand was unconditional negotiations between Buyoya and the Hutu rebels.
The decision at the summit came as Burundi's army said that Hutu rebels killed about 40 civilians, from both the majority Hutu and minority Tutsi populations, in the southern province of Bururi.
Buyoya has agreed to peace talks in principle but he and the Hutu rebels have so far not agreed to the other's conditions.

The leaders at the summit said they had a letter from Buyoya committing himself to unconditional negotiations with the Hutu National Council for the Defence of Democracy and other armed Hutu rebel groups.

"The summit agreed to appoint a ministerial committee made up of Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda and Cameroon to visit Burundi to ascertain Buyoya's committment to unconditional negotiations with other groups in Burundi," they said in a final statement.
"Non-compliance or obstruction of the negotiation process will lead to additional measures being taken against the regime and any of the factions," they warned.

But dangling the prospect of rewards for talks in front of Buyoya's military-appointed government, they added: "The summit also undertook to further respond positively should the regime enter into negotiation with all parties to the conflict."

Officials said Ethiopia, which has close ties to Washington, and Rwanda, considered the weakest link in sanctions because of ethnic sympathies, both suggested easing the embargo imposed in revenge for Buyoya seizing power in an army coup on July 25.
But others, led by Tanzania, Kenya and Zambia, argued giving way would only be rewarding Buyoya before he even began talks.
Reflecting their displeasure with Buyoya for using the army to oust civilian president Sylvestre Ntibantunganya, they met without him despite his request to be invited as head of state.
The summit consisted of the presidents of Kenya, Rwanda, Uganda, Tanzania, Zambia, the prime ministers of Ethiopia and Zaire and the secretary-general of the Organisation of African Unity (OAU).
Also attending the one-day talks were representatives of the United States and the European Union and former Tanzanian president Julius Nyerere, international mediator on Burundi.

U.S. officials said U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher made clear on Friday to East African leaders in Arusha the U.S. view that Buyoya had taken some positive steps by lifting bans on parliament and political parties in Burundi.

"The secretary in his discussions said, and others agreed, that there should be some effort to acknowledge progress when and as it is made," said a U.S. official travelling with Christopher, who flew on to Cape Town, South Africa, on Friday.
